content: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (PPROM) occurs in approximately 2% of pregnancies and can arise either spontaneously or as a result of medical interventions. PPROM is associated with several complications, including preterm birth, chorioamnionitis, neonatal sepsis, limb position abnormalities, respiratory distress syndrome, pulmonary hypoplasia, chronic lung disease, periventricular leukomalacia, and intraventricular hemorrhage. Various sealing techniques have been developed to restore the physical barrier against infection and promote the re-accumulation of amniotic fluid. However, the routine use of these sealants is not currently recommended due to insufficient evidence regarding their safety and efficacy. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of sealing techniques for PPROM compared to each other or to standard care (which may include no sealant) on maternal and neonatal outcomes. The review included randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials but excluded cluster-randomized trials and cross-over designs. Two studies involving 141 women (with data from 124 participants) were included in the review. Both studies were deemed to have a high risk of bias, and meta-analysis was not feasible due to differences in the interventions and outcomes reported. One study investigated the use of a cervical adapter (a mechanical sealing device) compared to standard care. This study, which included data from 35 participants, did not report on the primary outcome of perinatal mortality or most secondary outcomes for infants and mothers. There was no significant difference between the mechanical sealing group and the standard care group in terms of neonatal sepsis (risk ratio [RR] 1.19, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.28 to 5.09, very low-quality evidence) or chorioamnionitis (RR 1.19, 95% CI 0.28 to 5.09, very low-quality evidence). The second study examined the use of an oral immunological membrane sealant compared to standard care, with data from 94 participants. This study also did not report on the primary outcome of perinatal mortality or most secondary outcomes. However, the immunological membrane sealant was associated with a reduction in preterm birth before 37 weeks (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.68, very low-quality evidence) and neonatal death (RR 0.38, 95% CI 0.19 to 0.75, very low-quality evidence). There was no significant difference between the groups in terms of neonatal sepsis (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.28 to 1.46, very low-quality evidence) or respiratory distress syndrome (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.28 to 1.46, very low-quality evidence). The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of sealing procedures for PPROM. Neither of the included studies provided data on the primary outcome of perinatal mortality, and most secondary outcomes for infants and mothers were not reported. Limited evidence from one small study suggested that an immunological membrane sealant might reduce preterm birth before 37 weeks and neonatal death, but these findings should be interpreted cautiously due to the high risk of bias and lack of replication in other studies. Although mid-trimester PPROM is not uncommon, there is a scarcity of high-quality data on the benefits and risks of sealing procedures. Most available studies are retrospective or cohort-based and were therefore excluded from this review. The lack of prospective randomized trials in this area highlights the need for further research. Future studies should focus on randomized trials evaluating promising interventions, such as the amniopatch, and should assess outcomes including perinatal mortality, preterm birth, neonatal death, respiratory distress syndrome, neonatal sepsis, and developmental delay. Maternal outcomes, such as sepsis, mode of delivery, length of hospital stay, and emotional well-being, should also be evaluated.
